newsitem.title: USA: Cyprus ready for concessions to Turkish Cypriots.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus ready for concessions to Turkish Cypriots.

text.p: Cyprus' foreign minister pledged on Friday that his government would approach key talks over the divided island next month in a "spirit of give and take", ready to make concessions if the Turkish Cypriots did.

"We will go to the face-to-face negotiations with an open mind, having the political will to be constructive and positive and ready to negotiate a comprehensive solution to the Cyprus problem in a spirit of give and take," Ioannis Cassoulides said.
The Greek Cypriot government would be "ready to make concessions provided that this is based on the principle of reciprocity," Cassoulides told a news conference.
Greek and Turkish Cypriot leaders are expected to hold U.N.-sponsored talks on July 9 in New York, their first in three years, to try to end the 23-year division of Cyprus.

Cassoulides later met U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, two days after President Bill Clinton appointed Richard Holbrooke, negotiator of the 1995 Bosnia peace accord, as special emissary for Cyprus.

The minister hailed the appointment as showing that Washington "means business" in the search for a Cyprus settlement. Greek Cypriots hope the United States will put pressure on Turkey to be more flexible.
In a joint appearance before reporters, Albright assured Cassoulides "of America's interest in seeing the people of Cyprus achieve a lasting settlement to the inter-communal dispute on their island."
She said there could be "no more dramatic a demonstration of that commitment" than the appointment of Holbrooke.
"We believe that the division of the island is unacceptable," Albright added.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said that at the meeting, Albright noted U.S. "longstanding disagreement" with a decision by Cyprus to acquire Russian SA-10 anti-aircraft missiles.

Cyprus has promised not to start importing the missiles until next year, and Cassoulides noted earlier that if a Greek Cypriot proposal for demilitarization of the island was accepted, they would not be needed at all.

Burns also said Washington had expressed concern to Turkey over what Cyprus says was a violation of its airspace this week by three Turkish F-4 warplanes. He had said on Tuesday the United States did not know whether to believe the Cypriot charge or a Turkish denial.
Cassoulides said Cyprus was preparing for the New York talks despite feeling they could have been "better prepared" and concern they might end in failure, like previous talks.

"If negotiations were to collapse, this will increase the people's frustration since they have built expectations for a positive outcome." he said. "Similarly, it will erode the faith in the negotiating process and give an opportunity to hardliners from both sides to gain an advantage."
Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash, who will meet Cyprus President Glafcos Clerides in New York, had been inflexible during recent indirect preparatory talks, he charged.

Mainland Turkish troops invaded Cyprus in 1974 following a short-lived Greek Cypriot military coup in Nicosia. Some 30,000 troops remain in a Turkish-Cypriot mini-state that only Ankara recognises in the northern part of the island.
Both sides say they want to create a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation, but have never been able to agree the details.
